title: Electoral College
protagonist: Jane Earl, campaign manager for Paul Peaken
primary_metric: total projected electoral votes secured by Election Day within the fixed remaining travel budget (higher is better; both options must clear 270 to be a viable plan)

options.A: The Big-Prize Strategy -- concentrate the remaining travel budget in the highest-electoral-vote swing states (Florida, Pennsylvania) to put the largest possible number of electoral votes into play
options.B: The Margin Strategy -- concentrate the remaining travel budget in the narrowest-margin swing states, regardless of size, to win the largest number of separate states and spread the campaign's bet across several close races instead of one or two big ones

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC section 4

deliverables.text: A State Visit Budget Table -- every state visited, half/full day length, per-visit cost, running total against the remaining travel budget.

A Vote-Share Projection Table -- November 1 baseline plus the per-half-day swing rate, showing the one-step equation solved for the minimum half-days needed to exceed Farnsworth's share in that state.
An Electoral Vote Verification Table -- locked states plus flipped contested states, running EV total against the 270 threshold, and percent of all 538 electoral votes represented.
A Cost-Efficiency Comparison Table -- for all 37 contested states, dollar cost to flip, cost per electoral vote, and cost per percentage point flipped, ranked.
A Demographic Targeting Plan -- for every half day scheduled, the voter group targeted, justified with national demographic polling data.

balance.argument_a: Florida (30 EV) and Pennsylvania (19 EV) together put 49 electoral votes into play in two visits -- if both can be flipped, that single pair of states plus the locked 50 covers a large fraction of the road to 270 in the fewest number of distinct state-visit setups (minimizing the flat per-state travel cost paid only once per state).
balance.argument_b: Pennsylvania is tied at the poll (43/43), and Nevada (2-point gap) and Wisconsin (4-point gap) each need only 1-3 half-days to close -- the fewest of any states in Appendix C. Rather than betting the whole travel budget on two large, more-distant states, the Margin Strategy spreads it across three separate winnable contests: if a late-breaking event moves the polls against Peaken in any single state, the campaign still holds the others, and a win built from several states carries broader state-by-state momentum than a win built from two. This is a genuinely different rationale from dollar-efficiency, and it is not always the more dollar-efficient choice -- Nevada, for example, costs $150,000 per electoral vote flipped versus Texas's $32,500 (see D4), because a small state's flat per-state travel fee is spread across fewer electoral votes. The Margin Strategy's real case is breadth and resilience across many close races, not cost-per-vote.
balance.margin_basis: Computed via sensitivity_model.py (formula: 100*|A-B|/min(A,B), matching skills/case-readiness's own Tier 2 probe 5 convention): Strategy A (Big-Prize, greedy descending-EV among states Farnsworth currently leads or ties) reaches 296 total electoral votes spending the full $3,000,000 budget on Texas and Florida. Strategy B (Margin, greedy narrowest-current-gap-first among the same candidate states) reaches 261 electoral votes spending $2,700,000 on Pennsylvania (an exact tie, gap 0 -- the narrowest possible margin, needing only 1 half-day to strictly exceed Farnsworth once the model correctly treats a tie as not-yet-won), Nevada, and Wisconsin -- Michigan doesn't fit the remaining $300,000. Margin on the primary metric (total EV secured) = 13.4%, comfortably inside SPEC section 2's ~20% band; confirmed stable under the full mandated +/-50% flex on both stated assumptions (range 11.8%-12.4%, Strategy A wins every run). No constraint retuning was needed -- the original source's own $3,000,000/$19,000,000 figures are used unmodified.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Total remaining campaign funds and the advertising/travel split for the final week
modeling_assumptions.value_used: $19,000,000 total; $16,000,000 committed to advertising; $3,000,000 remaining for travel
modeling_assumptions.basis: Carried verbatim from the original case source document. Grounded in real order-of-magnitude campaign spending via [S5].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Case balance is not directly sensitive to the total; only the $3,000,000 remaining travel figure constrains state selection.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Flat per-state travel setup cost ($500,000) and per-visit cost ($200,000/half day, $400,000/full day)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Carried verbatim from the original case source document. Grounded in real order-of-magnitude campaign travel spending via [S7].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: One of the two most load-bearing assumptions in the case -- directly sets how many states/visits fit inside the $3,000,000 cap. Flagged for the +/-50% sensitivity flex (Tier 2 probe 3).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: 2 percentage points of a state's undecided pool shift to Peaken per half-day visit
modeling_assumptions.basis: Carried verbatim from the original case source document. Real research ([S6]) finds a real but unquantified, modest persuasion effect from campaign visits -- this case fixes one clean tractable number rather than presenting false precision.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The other most load-bearing assumption -- every D2 equation is built on it directly. Flagged for the +/-50% sensitivity flex (Tier 2 probe 3).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Appendix C's state-by-state poll numbers and Appendix D's national demographic poll numbers
modeling_assumptions.basis: Carried verbatim from the original case source document's own designed scenario data -- this is the case's own premise, not a real poll (a 2044 election has not occurred).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Data-integrity flag: Appendix D's 'White' column as re-transcribed does not reconcile to ~100% (F 49 + P 55 + N 12 = 116%) while every other column does (99-101%). Disclosed, not silently corrected. Does not affect the primary metric (electoral votes secured), only the non-primary D5 deliverable.

sensitivity_note: The 2%-per-half-day swing rate and the flat per-state travel cost are the case's most load-bearing assumptions -- both strategies' state selections are sensitive to how quickly a visit moves undecided voters and how much of the budget the flat per-state fee consumes. SPEC section 6 does not otherwise apply -- the case's stakes are political persuasion and vote share, not death/illness/financial hardship.

(2) P2 -- Option B (Margin Strategy) was framed as most-dollar-efficient but its own named example (Nevada at k/EV) was dominated by Texas (.5k/EV, outside Bs own selection set) -- redefined B around breadth/number-of-states-won instead, which its own 3-state example genuinely delivers vs As 2-state example; independently re-verified, all per-dollar language now explicitly disclaiming rather than claiming efficiency. (3) P6 -- S5 was mis-cited for a ,626,110 private-flight figure not present in the NBC article; re-sourced to the correct Fox News article that actually states this figure, independently re-verified via live fetch. P1 and P3 passed cleanly in the original run and were not re-verified since the fixes did not touch what they depend on. All 6 probes recorded, 0 FAIL.
